title: Negative doubles
source: Negative Double Hands Part 1.pdf, Negative Doubles Hands Part 2.pdf

deals.handout: South does not have enough high cards to bid his heart suit at the two-level, so he uses a negative double. North jumps to 2 NT to show 18-19 balanced points with spades stopped and fewer than 4 Hearts. South bids 3♥ to check for a heart fit, but with only 2 Hearts, North bids 3 NT.

problems.explanation: You have five hearts but only 7 HCP, not enough to bid 2♥. A negative double shows four or more hearts (and something in clubs) with 8 or more points at the two level, so it gets your hearts into the auction.

whyNot.2H: A new suit at the two level shows five or more cards and about 10 points. You have 7.
whyNot.P: With 7 HCP and five hearts, compete. The negative double shows your hearts.
whyNot.1N: 1NT over 1♠ promises a spade stopper. You have three small spades.

problems.explanation: Partner's double shows four or more hearts. You have only two. With 19 balanced and spades stopped, jump to 2NT: 18–19, a spade stopper, fewer than four hearts.

whyNot.1N: 1NT after a negative double shows a minimum, about 12–14. You have 19: jump.
whyNot.3N: Partner may have only 6 or 7 points. 2NT shows 18–19 and lets partner decide.
whyNot.2H: A heart bid shows four hearts. You have two.

problems.explanation: Partner's 2NT shows 18–19, so with 7 HCP you have enough for game. Partner has fewer than four hearts but may have three. Bid 3♥ to show five hearts, forcing, and partner chooses 4♥ or 3NT.

whyNot.3N: Partner may have three hearts, making a 5-3 fit. Show your fifth heart first.
whyNot.4H: Partner has fewer than four hearts, and may have only two. Let partner choose.
whyNot.P: 7 HCP opposite 18–19 is enough for game.

problems.explanation: Partner's 3♥ shows five hearts and asks whether you have three. You have two, so bid 3NT.

whyNot.4H: You have only two hearts: a seven-card fit at best. 3NT is the better game.
whyNot.P: 3♥ is forcing. Partner is asking about your heart length.

deals.handout: West is strong enough to bid at the two level, but with only 4 hearts must start with a double. East bids 2♥ showing 4 and West raises to game.

problems.explanation: You have 11 HCP, enough to bid at the two level, but only four hearts. 2♥ would promise five. Double instead: it shows four hearts, and you can bid game once partner shows a fit.

whyNot.2H: A new suit at the two level shows five or more cards and about 10 points. You have only four hearts.
whyNot.1N: 1NT promises a spade stopper. Yours are four small.
whyNot.P: With 11 HCP and four hearts you want to find a heart fit.

problems.explanation: Partner's negative double shows four hearts. You have four too, so bid 2♥ to show the fit. With a minimum, bid it at the lowest level.

whyNot.P: A negative double asks you to bid. With four hearts, show them.
whyNot.3H: Jumping shows extra values, about 15–17. You have 13.
whyNot.1N: You have a heart fit, and no spade stopper.

problems.explanation: Partner showed four hearts, and you have four: a fit. With 11 HCP and a singleton diamond opposite an opening bid, bid game.

whyNot.3H: With 11 HCP and a singleton opposite an opener, you have enough for game.
whyNot.P: You have a fit and enough for game.

deals.handout: North's negative double over 1D shows exactly 4-4 in the majors with 6 or more points. After South shows 4 spades, North has enough strength to jump to game in spades.

problems.explanation: After 1♣ and a 1♦ overcall, a negative double shows exactly four hearts and four spades. That's your hand. Find out which major partner has, then decide how high to go.

whyNot.1H: Bidding 1♥ could lose a 4-4 spade fit. Double shows both majors at once.
whyNot.1S: Bidding 1♠ could lose a 4-4 heart fit. Double shows both majors at once.
whyNot.3N: You might have a 4-4 major fit. Double to find out first.

acceptable.2S: A jump to 2♠ shows extra values, about 15–17. With 14 and a good club suit it's close; 1♠ is the simple choice.

problems.explanation: Partner's double shows exactly four cards in each major. You have four spades, so bid 1♠. Partner knows about the fit and will raise if there's more.

whyNot.1N: You have a four-card spade fit. Show it.
whyNot.2C: Show the spade fit first. Partner asked about the majors.
whyNot.1H: You have only two hearts. Bid the major where you have four.

problems.explanation: Partner has four spades and you have four: a fit. With 15 HCP opposite an opening bid, bid game.

whyNot.2S: With 15 HCP opposite an opener, you have enough for game.
whyNot.3S: With 15 HCP opposite an opener, don't just invite: bid game.
whyNot.3N: You've found the 4-4 spade fit. Play in spades.

deals.handout: South should use a negative double rather than bidding 4♦ because 3 NT is likely to be the right contract and a 4♦ bid would preclude a 3 NT contract. West is happy to bid 3 NT with a spade stopper and nothing else exciting to convey.
reviewNotes: The handout says "West is happy to bid 3 NT"; North bid it.

problems.explanation: Negative doubles apply through a 3♠ overcall. You have 11 HCP and length in both minors, but bidding 4♦ goes past 3NT, which is likely to be the best game. Double: it shows the unbid suits and enough to bid at the three level (9 or more), and partner can bid 3NT with a spade stopper.

whyNot.4D: 4♦ goes past 3NT, which is likely to be the best game.
whyNot.3N: You have no spade stopper. Let partner bid notrump.
whyNot.P: With 11 HCP you want to compete. Double shows your values and the unbid suits.

problems.explanation: Partner's double is negative: values and the unbid suits, clubs and diamonds. You have a spade stopper (A10) and nothing else to say, so bid 3NT.

whyNot.P: Passing turns partner's negative double into a penalty double. With only A10 of spades you can't expect to beat 3♠ by enough.
whyNot.4H: Your hearts are only five long and partner has shown short hearts. 3NT is the better game.
whyNot.4C: 4♣ goes past 3NT. With a spade stopper, bid it.

deals.handout: East makes a negative double showing four cards in each major. North has a promising minimum hand and bids his major at the 3 level. South has an easy raise to game.
reviewNotes: The handout says "East makes a negative double"; South did.

problems.explanation: After 1♣ and a 1♦ overcall, a negative double shows exactly four hearts and four spades. You have that, with 11 HCP.

whyNot.1H: Bidding 1♥ could lose a 4-4 spade fit. Double shows both majors at once.
whyNot.1S: Bidding 1♠ could lose a 4-4 heart fit. Double shows both majors at once.

problems.explanation: Partner's double shows four cards in each major, so you have a 4-4 spade fit. West's jump to 3♦ takes away your room, but with the fit and a good minimum, compete with 3♠.

whyNot.P: You have a four-card spade fit. Don't let the jump to 3♦ shut you out.
whyNot.4S: You have a minimum. Bid 3♠ and let partner decide about game.

problems.explanation: Partner bid 3♠ freely, over West's jump, so you have a 4-4 spade fit and partner has a decent hand. With 11 HCP and a singleton diamond, bid game.

whyNot.P: With 11 HCP, a singleton and a fit opposite an opener, bid game.

deals.handout: With 4 hearts East starts with a negative double. West bid 2H showing 4. East invites with 11 points and West has an easy accept.

problems.explanation: You have four hearts and 11 HCP. 2♥ would promise five, so double: it shows four hearts and at least 8 points.

whyNot.2H: A new suit at the two level shows five or more cards and about 10 points. You have only four hearts.
whyNot.1N: 1NT promises a spade stopper. You have three small spades.

problems.explanation: Partner's negative double shows four hearts. You have four, so bid 2♥ to show the fit.

whyNot.2D: You have a heart fit. Show it.
whyNot.3H: Jumping shows extra values, about 15–17. You have 13.
whyNot.P: A negative double asks you to bid. With four hearts, show them.

problems.explanation: You have a 4-4 heart fit, and partner has shown a minimum. You're a passed hand with 11 HCP, so invite with 3♥: partner bids game with a little extra.

whyNot.4H: Partner's 2♥ shows a minimum and you passed at your first turn. Invite and let partner decide.
whyNot.P: With 11 HCP and a fit, game is possible. Invite.

problems.explanation: Partner invited with 3♥. You have 13 HCP, a singleton club and a good five-card diamond suit: accept.

whyNot.P: Your shape makes your hand worth more than 13: accept the invitation.

deals.handout: East makes a negative double to show 4 hearts. West, without a second suit, and reluctant to bid 1 NT without a spade stopper rebids his 5 card diamond suit. East has spades stopped and an opening hand and tries 3 NT.

problems.explanation: You have four hearts and 14 HCP. Start with a negative double to look for a 4-4 heart fit. If partner doesn't have four hearts, you can bid 3NT next with your spade stopper.

whyNot.2H: A new suit at the two level shows five or more cards and about 10 points. You have only four hearts.
whyNot.3N: You might have a 4-4 heart fit. Double first, then bid 3NT if there isn't one.

problems.explanation: Partner's double shows four hearts, but you have only two. Without a spade stopper you can't bid notrump, and you have no second suit, so rebid your five diamonds.

whyNot.1N: 1NT promises a spade stopper. Yours are three small.
whyNot.2H: Raising hearts shows four. You have two.
whyNot.P: A negative double asks you to bid.

problems.explanation: Partner has no four hearts and no spade stopper. You have spades stopped (A654) and an opening hand, so bid 3NT.

whyNot.2N: 2NT would only invite. With 14 HCP opposite an opener, bid game.
whyNot.P: With 14 HCP opposite an opener, you have enough for game.

deals.handout: After the 1♥ overcall North doubles to show 4 spades (A 1♠ bid would show 5+ spades.) East raises hearts and south bids spades. North has 10 points but with bad values should not invite.

problems.explanation: Over a 1♥ overcall, a negative double shows exactly four spades. 1♠ would show five or more. You have four, so double.

whyNot.1S: 1♠ shows five or more spades. With exactly four, double.
whyNot.1N: With four spades, double first to look for a spade fit.

problems.explanation: Partner's double shows four spades. You have four too. East has raised hearts, so compete with 2♠. With a minimum, bid at the lowest level.

whyNot.P: You have a 4-4 spade fit. Compete.
whyNot.3S: Jumping shows extra values, about 15–17. You have 14.

problems.explanation: Partner has shown four spades and a minimum. You have 10 HCP, but no aces and a heart queen that may be worthless. Game is unlikely, so pass.

whyNot.3S: Partner's 2♠ is a minimum and your values are poor. Don't push.
whyNot.4S: Partner has a minimum. Game is unlikely.

deals.handout: The bids are straight-forward up to East's final bid. East may or may not bid 3♦. The shape is poor but the solid diamond suit suggests bidding.

problems.explanation: After 1♣ and a 1♦ overcall, a negative double shows exactly four hearts and four spades. You have that, with 7 HCP: enough at the one level.

whyNot.1H: Bidding 1♥ could lose a 4-4 spade fit. Double shows both majors at once.
whyNot.1S: Bidding 1♠ could lose a 4-4 heart fit. Double shows both majors at once.

problems.explanation: Partner's double shows four cards in each major. You have four spades, so there's a 4-4 fit. West has raised diamonds; compete with 2♠.

whyNot.P: You have a four-card spade fit. Compete.
whyNot.2H: You have three hearts and four spades. Bid the 4-4 fit.
whyNot.3S: Jumping shows extra values. You have a minimum.

deals.handout: With very strong spades and with North-South vulnerable, West should want to defend. West cannot double for penalties so he must pass and hope his partner can reopen with a double. East has good shape for a reopening double and West will convert for penalty.

problems.explanation: You'd like to double 1♠ for penalties, but playing negative doubles you can't: a double here would be negative. Pass, and hope partner reopens with a double, which you can pass for penalties.

whyNot.X: Double is negative, not penalty. Partner would bid, and you'd lose the chance to defend.
whyNot.1N: Possible, but with this spade holding you'd rather defend 1♠ doubled. Pass and hope partner reopens with a double.
whyNot.2D: Your diamonds are weak, and you'd rather defend.

problems.explanation: Partner passed 1♠, which may be because partner wanted to double it for penalties. With a singleton spade, reopen with a double: partner can pass to defend, or bid.

whyNot.P: Partner may be waiting to defend 1♠ doubled. With a singleton spade, reopen with a double.
whyNot.2H: A double keeps more options open: partner can pass for penalties, and you can still bid hearts later.

problems.explanation: Partner's reopening double gives you the chance you wanted. With AJ985 sitting over South's spades, pass to defend 1♠ doubled.

whyNot.2D: You wanted to defend 1♠ doubled, and now you can.
whyNot.1N: With this spade holding, defending 1♠ doubled pays more.

deals.handout: North has a minimum for a negative double at the 2 level. South has a nice hand and bids game.

problems.explanation: Over a 2♥ overcall, a negative double shows four spades and at least 8 points: you have exactly that. You don't have enough to bid 2♠.

whyNot.2S: 2♠ over 2♥ shows five or more spades and about 10 points. You have four, and 8.
whyNot.P: With four spades and 8 HCP, double to find a spade fit.
whyNot.2N: 2NT shows about 11–12 and a heart stopper. You have neither.

acceptable.3S: Inviting is reasonable with 16. But your good five-card club suit and the fit make game worth bidding.

problems.explanation: Partner's double shows four spades and at least 8 points. You have four spades and 16 HCP, with a good club suit. Bid game.

whyNot.2S: 2♠ shows a minimum. With 16 and a fit, bid more.

deals.handout: East's 1♠ bid shows a 5 card suit since he would use the negative double with only 4. West can jump to game with only 3 spades since that is enough to have an 8 card fit.

problems.explanation: Over a 1♥ overcall, a negative double shows exactly four spades. With five, bid 1♠: it shows five or more.

whyNot.X: Over 1♥, double shows exactly four spades. With five, bid them.
whyNot.1N: You have five spades. Show them.

problems.explanation: Partner's 1♠ shows five or more spades, since with four partner would have doubled. You have three, so there's an eight-card fit, and with 18 HCP you want game.

whyNot.2S: With 18 HCP, a raise to 2♠ undersells your hand. Bid game.
whyNot.3S: With 18 HCP and an eight-card fit, bid game.
whyNot.3N: Partner has five spades and you have three: play in the eight-card fit.

deals.handout: With a balanced hand and spades stopped North rebids 1 NT after the negative double.

problems.explanation: You have four hearts and 9 HCP. Over 1♠, a negative double shows four or more hearts, so it's the way to look for a heart fit.

whyNot.2H: A new suit at the two level shows five or more cards and about 10 points. You have only four hearts.
whyNot.1N: 1NT would hide your hearts. Double first.
whyNot.2D: A new suit at the two level shows five or more cards and about 10 points. You have four diamonds and 9 HCP.

problems.explanation: Partner's double shows four hearts. You have three, and a balanced minimum with spades stopped (K84). Bid 1NT: 12–14 balanced with a spade stopper.

whyNot.2H: Raising hearts shows four. You have three.
whyNot.2C: With a balanced hand and a spade stopper, 1NT describes it better.
whyNot.2N: A jump to 2NT shows 18–19. You have 14.

problems.explanation: Partner's 1NT shows 12–14 and denies four hearts. With 9 HCP you don't have enough for game, so pass.

whyNot.2N: Partner has 12–14. With 9, game is unlikely.

deals.handout: North makes a negative double of 1♥ showing exactly 4 spades. West might bid 3♥ or might sell out to 2♠.

problems.explanation: Over a 1♥ overcall, a negative double shows exactly four spades and, at the one level, 6 or more points. You have four spades and 7.

whyNot.1S: 1♠ shows five or more spades. With exactly four, double.
whyNot.P: With four spades and 7 HCP, compete.

problems.explanation: Partner's double shows four spades, and you have four. East has raised hearts, so compete with 2♠.

whyNot.P: You have a 4-4 spade fit. Compete.
whyNot.3S: Jumping shows extra values, about 15–17. You have 13.

deals.unusualSetup: The handout has West dealing board 7 (usually South deals it). The auction starts with West, so the deal follows the handout.
deals.handout: West's heart suit is not quite good enough for an opening 2 bid. After the 2♠ overcall, West should double to get the hearts into the auction. East rebids diamonds with a minimum opener and long diamonds, and West bids his long suit.
reviewNotes: West has 7 HCP, below the lesson's 9 for a negative double at the three level. The handout doubles anyway to get the six-card heart suit in; the problem follows the handout.

problems.explanation: You have six hearts but only 7 HCP. 3♥ would be forcing and show more. Double to get the hearts into the auction: if partner bids 3♦, you can bid 3♥ next, which shows long hearts without extra values.

whyNot.3H: A new suit at the three level is forcing and shows about 10 or more points. You have 7.
whyNot.P: With six hearts and a singleton diamond, get your hearts into the auction.

problems.explanation: Partner's double shows hearts. You have only two, and a minimum with six diamonds, so rebid 3♦.

whyNot.3H: Partner may have only four hearts. With two, rebid your long diamonds.
whyNot.P: A negative double asks you to bid.

problems.explanation: Partner has a minimum with long diamonds. You have six hearts, so bid 3♥. After your double, it shows long hearts and not enough to bid 3♥ at once.

whyNot.P: Diamonds is a poor fit. Your six hearts will play better.
whyNot.4H: Partner has shown a minimum, and you have 7 HCP.

deals.handout: South makes a negative double to show hearts since he doesn't have 5 of them. North rebids the diamonds and South raises to game in diamonds with a distributional hand and a big fit.

problems.explanation: You have four hearts. 2♥ would promise five, so start with a negative double to look for a heart fit. You can support diamonds later.

whyNot.2H: A new suit at the two level shows five or more cards and about 10 points. You have only four hearts.
whyNot.3D: A raise could lose a 4-4 heart fit. Double first.

problems.explanation: Partner's double shows four hearts. You have two, and a minimum with six good diamonds, so rebid 2♦.

whyNot.2H: Raising hearts shows four. You have two.
whyNot.1N: With six diamonds and a doubleton heart, rebid the diamonds.
whyNot.3D: Jumping shows extra values. You have a minimum.

problems.explanation: There's no heart fit, but you have five diamonds opposite partner's long suit, a singleton club and 12 HCP. You have no spade stopper for 3NT, so bid game in diamonds.

whyNot.3D: 3♦ only invites. With 12 HCP, a big fit and a singleton, bid game.
whyNot.4D: 4♦ isn't game. With 12 HCP and a big fit, bid it.
